idea: The core problem: there are infinitely many ways to accomplish almost anything — generate text, recognize images, recommend products, detect anomalies. Writing rules by hand would take forever and would break the moment circumstances shifted. So instead, you gather concrete examples of what you care about ("here are lesson plans we think are good"; "here is this person's behavior when they were healthy versus sick"; "these two songs are similar to each other") and ask the system to find the simplest pattern that fits all of them. The system becomes a pattern-completer: given new situations that *resemble* your examples in structure, it applies the same logic. Learning from examples works because a rule forced to fit many diverse, real-world instances has almost nowhere left to go wrong on fresh cases — the pattern has been crystallized by reality, not guessed from theory.
why: The mechanism rests on a hidden assumption: the world is simpler than it looks. If the true pattern connecting inputs to outputs is truly simpler than the raw noise in the data, and if your examples cover the major territory, then any rule general enough to fit all your examples will not have enough degrees of freedom left to be wildly wrong on new cases. Comparison (pulling similar things together, pushing different ones apart) works for the same reason — if two things are actually similar in the ways that matter, pulling them together reveals the hidden shared structure without anyone having to label what that structure *is*. The guarantee is not absolute: it only holds when the pattern is genuinely simpler than random, and when your examples are actually representative. Where it breaks: when the world is genuinely complicated (no simple pattern exists), when your examples are skewed or unrepresentative, or when the new case is far outside the territory your examples covered.
dots: Across the 40 papers, this idea takes on many disguises. In lesson planning (COMA) and emergency response training (SHIELD), systems learn the rhythm of good practice by observing multiple human examples and refining their output iteratively until it matches. In semi-supervised learning (the labeled-unlabeled graph paper), the system uses labeled nodes as anchors and then extracts the pattern from their neighborhoods to guess labels for the rest — it assumes similarity in the graph structure predicts similarity in true label. In recommendation (RaDAR, Adaptive Contrastive Learning), systems learn by generating multiple "views" of the same user-item interaction and comparing them — the invariant under different perturbations reveals what genuinely matters about a user. In anomaly detection (PAGE), the logic flips: normal data is the abundant example; artificial anomalies are created and contrasted against it. Few-shot learning (Glasses) solves the extreme case: with just a handful of labeled examples plus one target image, it adjusts a pre-trained model to generalize because the pre-training already found the broad strokes; the few examples fine-tune those strokes to the local context. Multimodal retrieval (Beyond Unimodal) aligns text and images by pulling descriptions toward images they describe; domain reranking (Domain-Specific Reranking) shows that a few hundred labeled examples within a domain beat massive out-of-domain pretraining because the small set, being *representative of what actually happens*, crystallizes the real pattern. The thread connecting them all: whether it is labeled examples, pairs of similar/dissimilar items, or examples of right versus wrong, the system is always asking the same question — what pattern unifies these cases I care about?
picture: Imagine a chef teaching a new cook to make pasta by showing them five dishes: one perfectly al dente, one overcooked, one with sauce that has broken, one with too much salt, one balanced. The cook doesn't memorize the exact ingredients or timing; they taste each one, feel the texture, see what went wrong or right, and slowly build intuition for what "done right" means. On the thousandth plate they make, they've never seen that exact combination of flour and humidity, but because they've internalized the pattern from those five examples and understood what balance feels like, they get it right. Learning from examples is the same: the system tasting examples, testing variations, and pulling together the pattern underneath them all.
